content:
the new float model does not relate floats to reals

Perhaps worth noting that for a long time we've had docs#Float.toRat?, but indeed until now it was not possible to prove theorems about it

It might not be possible to prove theorems about docs#Float.toRat? even after 4.33, as it is not listed among the supported operations in the post by @Julia Markus Himmel. In any case, my reading of the post is that Flocq port is the way to go.

In addition to the four existing projects that I listed above, there is also:

  1. HopfieldNet contains parts of Flocq-like floats.

Thanks for starting this discussion, and for mentioning FloatSpec :) I am the author of FloatSpec, and I would be very glad to see this new project move forward.

  1. FloatSpec is a faithful translation of Flocq. My starting point can be viewed as a cleaned-up version of a small part of this.

I agree that a Flocq-style layer relating floating-point objects to reals would be a useful complement to the new Lean float model, especially for numerical analysis and real-valued reasoning. If there are aspects of FloatSpec that currently make it hard to reuse, I would be happy to help refine them, clean up the structure, or introduce new features that would make it more useful for this effort.

In any case, I’m very happy to cooperate and contribute to the new project :)

One thing that I have wondered about FloatSpec is its use of Hoare triples. What is the rationale behind that?

As a starting point I looked into the proof that rounding produces a real in generic format, that is, Flocq's generic_format_round. Maybe I am just confused by the Hoare triples, but FloatSpec's generic_format_round doesn't look like the same statement. Contrary to Flocq's version, this seems to assume that x is in the format already before the rounding. (Note also that Flocq's generic_format_round and round_generic two distinct theorems, with two distinct proofs, see Generic_fmt.v)

Another thing that I wonder about FloatSpec is if it reproduces Flocq's structure too faithfully in places. For example, my understanding is that Raux and Zaux contain auxiliary facts about reals and integers. Are all these really needed given results in Mathlb?

What I would like to do is to reproduce some hand-picked results in Flocq using Mathlib as heavily as possible.
@Lauri Oksanen Have you been in contact with the original authors?

I am not entirely sure about the practical usage, so please explain based on specific use cases. I am particularly interested in verifying the equivalence of two different functions. Specifically, checking for functional identity between GPU kernels. Furthermore, I want to identify a formula that optimizes computational cost while remaining equivalent to the original under certain conditions.

  1. Suppose there are two functions using Float types. For example, fun a b = (2 * sin a + b) / 2 and fun a b = sin a + b / 2. While these would be mathematically identical if computed using Real types, let's assume a scenario where they might differ due to rounding errors (though I am not certain if these specific examples actually differ).
    How can I lift a from Float to Real to perform the proof?
    Conversely, how would I proceed with the proof if I were to lower a to FP8?
    What is the best way to effectively abstract the calculations? Do the frameworks provide support for this?

  2. How are types handled that lack NaN values—such as Posits—or types that resemble float but possess defined maximum and minimum values ​​(and also lack NaN)?

The new float model in Lean 4.33 won't cover trigonometric functions, see "Will you add my favorite operation?" in Himmel's post. For simpler operations such that addition, floats should behave as if the operation is performed with infinite precision and then rounded. This applies in the finite case. NaN and infinite values must be treated separately.

Proofs using the covered operations could work roughly like: prove for reals, prove rounding error bounds in the finite case, prove that the computations stay finite.

The basic Flocq-like model of floats is simple in the sense that it does not cover NaN and infinite values and it is unbounded. It should be fairly easy to relate the model to the finite part of UnpackedFloat, which is unbounded as well. However, the Flocq-like model doesn't see the difference between -0 and 0, so some care is needed.

The new float model in Lean 4.33 will be about traditional IEEE floats. Flocq is also aimed for them, though it is more abstract and other formats, such as fixed point numbers, are covered as well. It might not be general enough for Posits. I haven't thought about them. This is a direction different from relating reals and the new float model. It could be worthwhile to deviate from the Flocq-model if Posits require that.

@Lauri Oksanen :

Thanks, these are good points :)

On Hoare triples: the rationale was mostly historical/tooling-related. FloatSpec started as a translation effort where I wanted a uniform specification style that could also work for executable or monadic code via mvcgen. Also, Hoare triples make it easier for me (a new Lean learner at that time) to track prerequisites and requisites more clearly.

On generic_format_round: Flocq has two distinct theorems, round_generic and generic_format_round, and previous versions did have name mismatch issues. The current PR #8 has been corrected to reflect this split: round_generic/ roundR_generic is the identity theorem for already-generic inputs, while generic_format_round proves that rounding any real produces a generic-format value. Older compatibility wrappers around round_to_generic made this confusing, and that is exactly one of the things I would like to clean up.

I also agree about Raux and Zaux. The over-honest translation is mostly designed to ensure correctness of the repo, and some facts might be possible to be deleted.

Sorry for the delay in my reply, and happy to discuss further!

I came across the following which may be relevant:
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15965

I studied the formalization of the P3109 standard draft, thanks @Ching-Tsun Chou. I think the standard can be covered by the Flocq-model with minor modifications. The standard does not include posits. My opinion is that posits should be out of scope of this project. They don't seem to be adopted widely. (But please correct me if I am wrong.)

The clamping (or saturation) of P3109 is different from IEEE-754, but the Flocq-philosophy of round first then clamp applies, see project of the FLoPS formalization of the standard. I have focused on rounding for the moment.

Two generalizations are needed:

  1. The stochastic rounding of P3109 is not monotone, so we must relax the valid rounding predicate of Flocq. A lot of theory can be proven assuming only Faithfulness. Stochasticity can be modeled in "oracle style" as in FLoPS.
  2. When precision is 1, the P3109 tie break when rounding to nearest does not fit into Flocq-style rounding that depends only on the significand. FLoPS solves the issue by letting rounding depend on both exponent and significand. I propose a different approach based on an abstraction and dealing with the corner case separately as in this sketch.
